column1: What are the four fundamental elements of a classical feedback control architecture?
column2: Plant (physical process), sensor (measures output), controller (computes corrective action from error), and actuator (applies force/heat/voltage/flow to the plant).

column1: For a first-order low-pass filter with time constant τ and DC gain K, what is the Laplace-domain transfer function, and where is its pole located?
column2: H(s) = K/(τs + 1); the pole is at s = -1/τ, which also sets the -3dB cutoff frequency at ω = 1/τ.

column1: What is the fundamental design tension in control loop tuning regarding responsiveness?
column2: A system reacting too aggressively overshoots and oscillates (risking instability/actuator saturation), while one too conservative lags, fails to reject disturbances, and converges too slowly.

column1: What is the core invariant regarding raw sensor outputs in industrial measurement?
column2: Raw sensor outputs are almost never immediately usable—they are weak, noisy, and nonlinear, and must be conditioned before an ADC or digital input can reliably interpret them.

column1: Why is calibration considered a recurring process rather than a one-time event in industrial sensing?
column2: Sensors drift over time due to thermal effects, mechanical hysteresis, and material degradation, requiring periodic recalibration, redundancy, and statistical outlier rejection.

column1: What signal format does a typical industrial pressure transducer use for transmission, and why?
column2: A 4–20 mA current loop, chosen because current signals resist noise/voltage-drop degradation over long cable runs better than voltage signals.

column1: Describe the five sequential steps of the PLC scan cycle.
column2: 1) Read all physical inputs, 2) execute user program (ladder logic) rung-by-rung in sequence, 3) write all outputs, 4) perform housekeeping/diagnostics, 5) repeat.

column1: What is the historical origin of ladder logic notation, and why did it succeed in industrial adoption?
column2: It originated from 1950s–60s relay schematic diagrams (power rails, contacts, coils); it succeeded because electricians could read/troubleshoot it without learning formal computer programming.

column1: What core architectural problem do SCADA and DCS systems solve?
column2: Spatial decoupling with temporal synchronization—coordinating geographically dispersed equipment while giving operators real-time visibility and control, avoiding single points of failure from centralized wiring/control.

column1: In hierarchical industrial control architecture, how do field-layer and supervisory-layer cycle times differ?
column2: Field layer (PLCs, RTUs, IEDs) executes real-time loops at ~10–100 ms; the supervisory layer (HMI, historian, engineering stations) operates on longer timescales of ~500 ms to several seconds.

column1: Why do industrial fieldbus protocols often eliminate the OSI session, presentation, and transport layers?
column2: Because each abstraction layer adds latency/overhead; with real-time cycle targets in the hundreds of microseconds, protocols implement application semantics directly atop the data link layer to meet deterministic timing.

column1: What is the key distinction between a Basic Process Control System (BPCS) and a Safety Instrumented System (SIS) under IEC 61511?
column2: The BPCS optimizes normal process operation/efficiency, while the SIS provides independent risk reduction with a defined Safety Integrity Level (SIL), targeting a specific probability of dangerous failure on demand.
